Findings.Description: The resolved specification's Summary and one acceptance criterion cite the human decision as 'specification-001', but the actual DecisionId supplied is 'specification-review-001'. This is a traceability mismatch between the resolved spec and the source decision record.
Findings.Evidence: HUMAN DECISION.DecisionId = 'specification-review-001'; resolved Summary says 'per human decision specification-001'; the café acceptance criterion says 'per Unicode-aware classification decision specification-001'.
Findings.Recommendation: Correct all references to the decision ID so they consistently read 'specification-review-001' (or whatever the canonical ID is).

Findings.Description: The apostrophe OpenQuestion is not genuinely unresolved: the stated word definition (letters or digits only, no exceptions) already unambiguously classifies apostrophe as a non-letter/non-digit separator, and the entry itself states this conclusion as a firm 'Assumption ... per the stated definition with no exceptions.' This reads as a resolved rule masquerading as an open question rather than a genuine ambiguity.
Findings.Evidence: OpenQuestions: "Should apostrophes within words (e.g., \"don't\") be treated as separators ... Assumption: apostrophe is not a letter/digit, so it acts as a separator (\"don't\" -> 2 words), per the stated definition with no exceptions."
Findings.Recommendation: Move this resolved behavior into Requirements/AcceptanceCriteria (e.g., add an explicit acceptance criterion for "don't" -> 2) and remove it from OpenQuestions, or keep it only if there is a genuine reason to doubt the no-exceptions reading.

Findings.Description: The Requirements text explicitly claims support for non-Latin scripts (Cyrillic, CJK) and non-ASCII decimal digits as valid word characters, per the human decision's Unicode-aware intent, but no AcceptanceCriteria exercise these cases. Only Latin-script accented letters (café, naïve) are tested. This leaves the broader Unicode claim underspecified for downstream test generation.
Findings.Evidence: Requirements: "This includes accented letters, non-Latin scripts (e.g., Cyrillic, CJK), and non-ASCII decimal digits as valid word characters." No AcceptanceCriteria example uses Cyrillic, CJK, or non-ASCII digits (e.g., Arabic-Indic digits).
Findings.Recommendation: Add at least one acceptance criterion each for a Cyrillic word, a CJK run, and a non-ASCII digit run to make the Unicode-aware claim independently testable.

Findings.Description: Under char.IsLetterOrDigit semantics, scripts written without inter-word whitespace (e.g., CJK) will have an entire contiguous run of ideographs counted as a single 'word', since each character is individually a Unicode letter. This is a legitimate but non-obvious consequence of the human decision that is neither called out nor tested, and could surprise consumers who expect 'word count' to align with linguistic word boundaries in such scripts.
Findings.Evidence: Requirements state CJK characters are valid word characters with no accompanying discussion of word segmentation for scripts lacking whitespace delimiters; no acceptance criterion demonstrates this behavior.
Findings.Recommendation: Either explicitly document this consequence as intended behavior (a whole unspaced CJK run = 1 word) with a supporting acceptance criterion, or clarify if a different segmentation is actually desired for such scripts.

Findings.Description: The Requirements state Unicode-awareness is 'equivalent to char.IsLetterOrDigit', which operates per UTF-16 code unit. For characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (surrogate pairs), each half of the pair is classified as a Surrogate, not a Letter or Digit, so a naive per-char implementation would fail to count supplementary-plane letters/digits as word characters — understating the 'Unicode-aware' claim. This is already flagged in OpenQuestions but is worth surfacing explicitly since it creates a latent gap between the normative wording and true full-Unicode behavior.
Findings.Evidence: Requirements: "using Unicode-aware classification (equivalent to char.IsLetterOrDigit)"; OpenQuestions: "Should CountWords have any handling for surrogate pairs / astral-plane Unicode characters ... or is basic char-by-char iteration via char.IsLetterOrDigit sufficient given the Unicode-aware classification decision?"
Findings.Recommendation: Resolve this open question before implementation if supplementary-plane characters are in scope; otherwise explicitly scope the Unicode-aware guarantee to the BMP to avoid an implementation/spec mismatch.

Summary: The resolved specification faithfully carries the original requirement forward and correctly incorporates the human decision (Unicode-aware char.IsLetterOrDigit-based classification) into both the normative Requirements and the AcceptanceCriteria, including two accented-letter examples (café, naïve) that were independently re-derived and confirmed correct. All 16 acceptance criteria were independently recomputed against the stated word definition and match the specified expected values; no contradictions between requirements, examples, and definitions were found, and no corrupted/replacement-character literals (e.g., U+FFFD) were detected. Remaining issues are non-blocking: a decision-ID citation mismatch, one OpenQuestion (apostrophes) that is actually already resolved by the base definition and should be promoted into the normative text, and two testability gaps where the broadened Unicode claim (non-Latin scripts, non-ASCII digits, and the resulting CJK single-word-run behavior) is asserted but not covered by any acceptance criterion, plus a lingering ambiguity around supplementary-plane (surrogate pair) handling that is already tracked as an open question. None of these block downstream test generation for the currently specified ASCII/BMP-Latin cases, but the omissions should be closed before claiming full Unicode coverage is verified.
